facts.fact_text: In its judgment of 17 May 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice found that since the demonstrations organised by the CDPP had been illegal, the sanction imposed on it had not been disproportionate.
The gatherings shown in the video submitted by the Government were held in Great National Assembly Square, in a pedestrian area, in front of the government buildings.
The participants in the gatherings shown in the video appeared to number several hundred and included people of different ages varying from schoolchildren to pensioners.
During the gatherings shown in the video, different personalities made speeches critical of the ruling Communist Party, the government and its policy.
No signs of violence can be seen in the video submitted by the Government of the gatherings held on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.
'The Layabout's Anthem' (Imnul Golanilor — a song that originated in the 1990 Bucharest student demonstrations) was played frequently at the gatherings shown in the video.

The chorus of 'The Layabout's Anthem' (Imnul Golanilor) included the following lines: 'I'd rather be a slacker than a traitor (Mai bine haimana, decât trădător) / I'd rather be a hooligan than a dictator (Mai bine huligan, decât dictator) / I'd rather be a layabout than an activist (Mai bine golan, decât activist) / I'd rather be dead than a communist (Mai bine mort, decât comunist).'
On 9 January 2002, the parliamentary group of the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) held a gathering in Great National Assembly Square, in front of government headquarters.
The parliamentary group of the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) also held gatherings on 11, 13, 15, 16 and 17 January 2002.

By a decision of 3 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council classified the gathering to be held on 9 January 2002 as a 'demonstration' within the meaning of sections 4, 8, 12 and 13 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995.

By a decision of 3 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council authorised the parliamentary group of the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) to hold the gathering on 9 January 2002 in National Opera Square rather than Great National Assembly Square.

In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice stated that the CDPP had breached the provisions of section 6 of the Assemblies Act by organising demonstrations in Great National Assembly Square on 9, 10, 11 and 13 January 2002.

In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice stated that the CDPP had organised demonstrations in Great National Assembly Square notwithstanding that the authorisation issued by Chișinău Municipal Council only gave permission for a demonstration on 9 January 2002 in National Opera Square.
In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice called for an immediate halt to the gatherings, which it considered to be illegal and unconstitutional.

In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice warned the CDPP that if it failed to comply with the warning, the Ministry would impose a temporary ban (suspendarea activităţii) on the party's activities in accordance with section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act.

On 18 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice issued a decision imposing a one-month ban on the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP)'s activities, in accordance with section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991.
The one-month ban on the CDPP's activities imposed on 18 January 2002 was based on the organisation by the CDPP of unauthorised demonstrations on 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16 and 17 January 2002.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the CDPP had breached the provisions of sections 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 11 of the Assemblies Act by not obtaining prior authorisation from Chișinău Municipal Council to stage demonstrations.
According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the CDPP had breached the provisions of sections 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 11 of the Assemblies Act by blocking the public highway.

Section 5 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted only after the organisers have notified the local council.
Section 11(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that not later than fifteen days prior to the date of the assembly, the organiser shall submit a notification to the Municipal Council.

Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate: the name of the organiser and the aim of the assembly; the date, starting time and finishing time; the location and the access and return routes; the manner in which the assembly is to take place; the approximate number of participants; the persons who are to ensure and answer for the sound conduct of the assembly; and the services the organiser asks the Municipal Council to provide.

The amended section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act (as amended on 21 November 2003) provides that during the temporary ban, it shall be forbidden for the party to use the mass media, to disseminate propaganda and publicity, to carry out bank transactions or other operations in respect of its assets and to participate in elections.

Section 6(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be conducted peacefully, without any sort of weapons, and shall ensure the protection of participants and the environment, without impeding the normal use of public highways, road traffic and the operation of economic undertakings and without degenerating into acts of violence capable of endangering the public order and the physical integrity and life of persons or their property.

Section 8(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted in squares, streets, parks and other public places in cities, towns and villages, and also in public buildings.

Section 8(3)(a) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within fifty metres of the parliament building, the residence of the President of Moldova, the seat of the government, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of Justice.

Section 8(3)(b) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within twenty-five metres of the buildings of the central administrative authority, the local public authorities, courts, prosecutors' offices, police stations, prisons and social rehabilitation institutions, military installations, railway stations, airports, hospitals, companies which use dangerous equipment and machines, and diplomatic institutions.

Article 32(3) of the Constitution of the Republic of Moldova provides that denial and defamation of the State and of the people, incitement to war of aggression, incitement to hatred on ethnic, racial or religious grounds, incitement to discrimination, territorial separatism or public violence, as well as other acts undermining the constitutional order shall be forbidden and shall be punishable under the law.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal stated that as a result of the CDPP demonstrations, the public transport company had suffered losses of 12,133 Moldovan lei (MDL), equivalent to approximately 1,050 euros (EUR) at the time.
In its judgment of 17 May 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice found that since the demonstrations organised by the CDPP had been illegal, the sanction imposed on it had not been disproportionate.

In its ruling of 25 February 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice stated that even if the CDPP had the initial intention of holding meetings with its supporters, those meetings later took on the character of demonstrations, marches, processions and picketing, which fall under the provisions of the Assemblies Act, and that the leaders of the CDPP were therefore required to comply with the provisions of the Assemblies Act.
It appears from the video submitted by the Government that traffic was not disrupted as a result of the gatherings held on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.
The Ministry of Justice did not reply to Chișinău Municipal Council's request of 23 January 2002 for interpretation of the law.
The Ministry of Justice did not address any request to Parliament for an official interpretation of the legislation, as requested by Chișinău Municipal Council on 23 January 2002.
